After we have covered all of the information about each group, an experiment is provided to demonstrate the instructions.
Let's begin the lesson on MOVE AND BRANCH COMMANDS........................
Before getting into the individual Move instructions, we must first cover the method in which data is referenced in the 68000 microprocessor, the Addressing Mode.

When accessing data you refer to it through an addressing mode. The 68000 microprocessor has 14 Addressing Modes. Not all instructions implement all Addressing Modes. Some may even support only a few. Let's look at each of the modes.
This method is used when you want to use data that is stored in a data register.
For example, a Data Register Direct to Data Register Direct move instruction could look like this: MOVE.L D1,D0. This instruction says move the long word contents of D1 into D0.
The Address Register Direct method is used when you want to use the data in an address register.
For example, MOVEA.L $00011000,A1, loads the hex value 00011000 into the A1 register..
This method, also known as ABS, is used to indicate a short address in memory. A short address is a word size address.

For example MOVE.W $100,D1 moves the word size content of data at memory location $100 into D1. Note, if the short address value is greater than 7FFF, all the upper bits of the address will be set to one.
The processor, even though you are passing a word size value, still works on 32 bits. For numbers from $0000 to $7FFF all higher bits are zero, from $8000 to $FFFF all higher bits are set to one.
The Absolute Long is the same as the Absolute Short, except for the data in the instruction is two words long.
There are no higher bit differences because the maximum address size will be specified. An example of an Absolute Long instruction would be MOVE.L $33C4AA12,D1.
This instruction will load the long word data at location $33C4AA12 and store it in D1.
Address Register Indirect addressing uses data pointed to by the value stored in the indicated address register.
For example, if A1 contained $00000100, the instruction MOVE.B (A1),D1 would move the value in memory at location $100 and store it in D1.
This method works the same as the Address Register Indirect with one exception: the address register is incremented after it is used.
The instruction looks like this: MOVE.B (A1)+,D1. Note that there is no Preincrement addressing mode.
This method works the same as the Address Register Indirect with one exception: the address register is decremented before it is used.
The instruction looks like this: MOVE.B -(A1),D1. Note that there is no Postdecrement addressing mode.
This method works the same as the Address Register Indirect with one exception: the address register is displaced by a certain value and the data at that location is used.
The address in the address register is unchanged. It was only displaced during the read. The instruction for this looks like: MOVE.B $1F(A2),D3.
This method works the same as the Indirect with Displacement with one addition.
A displacement is still used, but the value of a data register or address register is also used to displace the value in the address register. This secondary register is known as an index.
The format for this addressing mode is: MOVE.B 4(A2,D2.B),D1. In this example, D2 byte size value is the index which is added to A2 along with the value of 4.
This mode works the same as Indirect with Displacement with one exception: an address register is not used; the program counter is used. An example would be: MOVE.W $F(PC),D5.
This mode works the same as Indirect with Index with one exception: an address register is not used; the program counter is used. An example would be: MOVE.W
This addressing mode means that the data follows the instruction in memory before the next instruction.
For example, MOVE.W #$FFFF,D1 indicates that the data $FFFF is moved into D1. The value with a # in front of it indicates immediate.
In this addressing mode the data is within the instruction and is usually only 4 bits long.
This addressing method uses a name to identify the source, destination, or operands.
Example names would be SR (Status Register), USP (User Stack Pointer), PC (Program Counter) or SSP (Supervisor Stack Pointer). An example instruction would be: MOVE.W SR,D1.
It is important to at least recognize the different addressing modes. They are not used just for the MOVE or BRANCH commands, but are used in a variety of different instructions.
Now that you have a basic understanding of the modes, the MOVE instruction will be easier to understand.
Which addressing mode uses data as a pointer to data in a different location?
The addressing mode you have chosen does not work this way, it uses the data directly, not as a reference to other data.
There are 11 move commands in the 68000 instruction set. The table below shows these instructions, an example of its use, and any addressing modes not supported in the source or destination.

Move is probably the most common instruction in the MOVE group. The table on the previous page indicates what addressing modes are allowed for the source and destination. The instruction format is: MOVE.SIZE SOURCE,DESTINATION
Size is B, W, or L (byte size, word size or longword size.) When the data is moved from the source to the destination, it is analyzed by the microprocessor.
The analysis causes certain indications in the condition code register (lower half of status register). The X (extend) bit is unaffected. N (negative) is set if the value being moved is negative.
Z (zero) is set if the value is zero and V (overflow) and C (carry) are always set to 0. The figure below shows the encoding of this instruction into machine language.
The Move to SR instruction can only be used in the supervisor mode. The instruction format is: MOVE.W SOURCE,SR
The only data size allowed is word, because the status register is only 1 word in length. Normally, this move can be used with the MOVE from SR to change the status register settings.

The status register is read, the bits to be changed are masked, and the value is then reloaded into the SR. The Move to SR instruction does not modify any of the condition codes in the status register.
The Move from SR instruction can only be used in the supervisor mode. The instruction format is: MOVE.W SR,DESTINATION
The only data size allowed is word, because the status register is only 1 word in length. Normally, this move can be used with MOVE to SR to change the status register settings.
The status register is read, the bits to be changed are masked, and the value is then reloaded into the SR. This instruction does not change the contents of the condition codes.
The Move to CCR instruction can be used in both Supervisor and User modes. The format for this instruction is:
The data size for this instruction is word, however, the first byte is ignored and the lower byte is loaded into the CCR. Remember, the CCR is the Condition Code Register.
You can use this move command to set the values of the Condition Code. The figure below shows the MOVE from SR machine language encoding.
The Move from CCR instruction can also be used by programs executed in the User and Supervisor modes. The format for this instruction is: MOVE.W CCR,DESTINATION
The only data size allowed is word. The destination will contain all zeros in the upper byte with the conditional code in the lower byte.
This instruction is useful when the contents of the Condition Codes are needed as a whole. The figure below shows the machine language encoding for this instruction:
This instruction may only be used in the Supervisor Mode. If used in User Mode a privilege violation will occur. The instruction format is: MOVE.L ADDRESS REGISTER,USP
The only data size allowed is a long word. This instruction takes the address stored in a specified address register and loads it into the User Stack Pointer.
The User Stack Pointer now refers to a different memory location. The figure below shows the MOVE to USP machine language encoding.
This instruction may only be used in the Supervisor Mode. If used in User Mode a privilege violation will occur. The instruction format is: MOVE.L USP,ADDRESS REGISTER

The only data size allowed is a long word. This instruction takes the address stored in the User Stack Pointer and loads it into a specified address register. The User Stack Pointer remains unchanged.
This instruction is the Move Address Instruction and can be used in either processor modes. The instruction format is: MOVE.SIZE SOURCE,ADDRESS REGISTER
This instruction data size can be either word or long word. The normal Move command does not allow moving data into an Address Register Direction. This instruction allows this function.
This is a very useful instruction, which you will see later acts similar to LEA (Load Effective Address) for certain addressing modes. The figure below shows the MOVEA machine language encoding.
This instruction is the Move Multiple Register instruction and can be used in either processor modes. The instruction format is: MOVE.SIZE REGISTER LIST,DESTINATION

This instruction data size can be either word or longword. This instruction is used to either move certain registers to consecutive memory location or move data at consecutive memory locations into certain registers.
The instruction is followed by a word containing the encoded information for which register values are being moved. The mask order depends on the format of the instruction you are using.

This instruction is the Move Peripheral Data instruction and can be used in either processor modes. The instruction format is: MOVE.SIZE DATA REGISTER,INDIRECT WITH DISPLACEMENT MOVE.SIZE INDIRECT WITH DISPLACEMENT,DATA REGISTER
This instruction data size can be either word or longword. This instruction is used in moving data to peripheral devices which are 8-bit and not 16.

By specifying an even address, each byte of data is sent through the upper byte of the data bus starting with the highest byte. Likewise, an odd address will cause the data to be sent through the lower 8 data lines of the data bus.
This instruction is the Move Quick instruction and can be used in either processor modes. The instruction format is:
This instruction data size can be longword only. This instruction is used to move an eight byte data quickly into a data register.
Since the instruction is longword size only, the MSB determines all of the higher bits. In other words if bit 7 is high, bit 8-31 will be high.
If bit 7 is low, all upper bits will be low in the data that is put into the data register. The condition codes are set under the same circumstances as the MOVE instruction.
The Move instructions are very important. Microprocessors can only perform arithmetic and logical functions with some of the data in the microprocessor registers.
Move commands are used to load in and out data that you are using. In the experiment you will see the use of a Move command.
This completes the information on MOVE COMMANDS.TLE........

There are 9 branch commands in the 68000 instruction set. The table below shows each of these instructions, an example of its use, and any addressing modes not supported in the instruction.
Remember that the Addressing Mode information is contained in the section about the Move instructions.
The Bcc instruction is for branching based on a condition. The format for this instruction is shown below:
Size is B or W. This size indicates the Displacement size. The Displacement value is a two's-complement number that is added to the program counter if the condition being tested is true.
This way, when the microprocessor looks at the PC for the next instruction, it looks at this new location. The condition you are checking depends on what you substitute for cc.
For example, the BCS branches to the new location only if the carry bit is set to one. The BCC only branches if the carry bit is zero.
You probably see that the branching location is limited to the Displacement value that you can add to the program counter.
The condition codes are not modified after the use of this instruction.
The BRA instruction is for the branching always. The format for this instruction is shown below: BRA. SIZE DISPLACEMENT
Size is B or W. This size indicates the Displacement size. The Displacement value is a two's-complement number that is added to the program counter.

This way, when the microprocessor looks at the PC for the next instruction, it looks at this new location. You probably see that the branching location is limited to the Displacement value that you can add to the program counter.

It is important to note that their isn't any condition being tested; this instruction always branches when executed. Again, this instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the status register.
The BSR instruction is used to branch a subroutine. The format for this instruction is shown below:
Size is B or W. This size indicates the Displacement size. The Displacement value is a two's-complement number that is added to the program counter.
This way, when the microprocessor looks at the PC for the next instruction, it looks at this new location. The figure below shows the encoding for this instruction.
You probably see that the branching location is limited to the displacement value that you can add to the program counter.
It is important to note that their isn't any condition being tested, this instruction always branches when executed.
The difference between this instruction and the BRA instruction is that this instruction stores the PC value on the stack before adding the displacement.
Again, this instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the status register.
The DBcc instruction is for testing a condition, decrementing, and branching. The format for this instruction is shown below: DBcc. DATA REGISTER,SIZE DISPLACEMENT
Size is B or W. This size indicates the Displacement size. The Displacement value is a two's-complement number that is added to the program counter.
This way, when the microprocessor looks at the PC for the next instruction, it looks at this new location. This branching instruction is used primarily for loops.
The Displacement is back to the start of the loop. When the process gets to this instruction it tests the condition. If the condition is true, then the processor moves on to the next instruction.
If the condition is false then the processor subtracts 1 from the specified Data Register contents. If the Data Register does not equal -1 then it adds the Displacement to the PC.
Again, this instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the Status Register.
The JMP instruction is for jumping. The format for this instruction is shown below: JMP DESTINATION
This instruction jumps to the specified location. The difference between this instruction and BRA is that the value is not a Displacement, so the jump to location is not limited.
This instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the Status Register..
The JSR instruction is for Jumping to a Subroutine. The format for this instruction is shown below: JSR DESTINATION
This instruction Jumps to the specified location. The difference between this instruction and BSR is that the value is not a Displacement, so the Jump to location is not limited.
This instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the Status Register.
The RTE instruction is for Returning from an Exception. The format for this instruction is shown below: RTE

When certain exceptions occur, the Status Register and Program Counter values are stored on the stack. This instruction, when evaluating exception processing code, can return to the location immediately after the exception.
Note that not all exceptions can use the RTE instruction. This instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the Status Register.
The RTS instruction is for returning from a subroutine. The format for this instruction is shown below: RTS
When using BSR or JSR instructions, once you finish your subroutine you can use the RTS command to go back to the instruction immediately after the BSR or JSR.
Remember that in your subroutine, when data is placed on a stack it must be taken off. This leaves the PC value (placed by the BSR or JSR instruction) last on the stack.
This instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the status register.
The RTR instruction is for Returning from a Subroutine and Restoring condition codes. The format for this instruction is shown below: RTR

When using BSR or JSR instructions, if you push the condition codes to the stack first, and your subroutine is finished, you can use the RTR command to go back to the instruction immediately after the BSR or JSR instruction. This will restore the previous condition code values.
In your subroutine, when data is placed on a stack it must be taken off. This leaves the PC value (placed by the BSR or JSR instruction) last on the stack.
This instruction does not change any of the condition codes in the status register.
Branch instructions are used extensively in modular programs.
You have probably seen many of these branch instructions in code that you have entered into the 68000 microprocessor trainer.

In this experiment we will carefully look at a short segment of code. The code you will enter uses some of the instructions introduced in the theory section of this lesson. lesson.lesson.
1. Set the Test Console controls to the initial control settings..........

2. Carefully insert the PC130-468 card into the PC1 position, the PC130-403 card into the PC2 position, the PC130-401 card into the PC3 position and place the PC130-404 card in front of the test console.
3. Set the Positive Supply Voltage to 5 volts.............................

4. Using the 50-pin short cable, connect PC1 J1 and PC2 J2 together. Remember to align the red wire side of the cable with the end of the connectors labeled either "1" or "2" on all ribbon cable connections.
5. Using the 20-pin short cable, connect PC2 J2 and PC3 J1 together. Remember to follow the red wire and 1 on the circuit boards.
6. Using the 20-pin long cable, connect PC3 J2 and the Keyboard and Display J1 together. Remember to follow the red wire and 1 on the circuit boards.
Program 1 shows the code that you will enter. Line numbers are provided on each line of the code to easily identify the instruction we are talking about.
The first line of code is a MOVEA instruction. The value of $00040000 will be stored in address register 1. This address is the address of parallel port A.
The next line of code uses immediate decimal data and stores it Data Register Direct to D1. The Move.B #$10,D0 moves the byte size immediate hex data 10 into D0.
Line 4, Move.B D1,(A1) uses data register direct and indirect. The byte size data in D1 is sent to the address of A1, in this case port A.

Line 5 is a decrement and branch if not equal. This instruction will decrement D0 as long as the condition is false. If D0 gets to 1, the branch displacement will no longer occur and the microprocessor will move on.
The last line, 6, is used to return to the monitor program. The monitor program runs routines as if they were subroutines.
1. Press the Reset key on the PC130-468 card. The main screen of the monitor program should be displayed.
2. Press the EDIT key and enter the value "11000". Enter the program shown below. Remember, to be careful when entering in the values.
3. Once you have finished entering the code, press the STOP key, press the RUN key on the 68000 keypad and enter the address value "11000". Press ENTER after doing so.
Observe the display of the 68000. The display should say "Program Terminated Correctly." This indicates that the RTS instruction worked at the end of the program.
If you look at port A on card PC130-401 (the bottom of the three LED arrays) you should see the number value 5 encoded in binary on the LEDS.
Try changing the values using edit and see if you can get other values to display.
Now you have seen the direct operation of move and branch commands. Feel free to explore different instructions using the information presented earlier in this lesson.
You will quickly discover what you can change and what effects it causes in the program operation.
